newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-CoreLab tracks oil industry path.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-CoreLab tracks oil industry path.

text.p: Core Laboratories hopes to triple its revenues to $300 million in the next three years as it capitalizes on a restructuring in the oil industry that has led to more outsourcing of services and to greater environmental risk management, its president and chief executive said.

The Houston-based company has seen its revenues grow to $100 million this year from $69 million in 1994, and wants to fuel 20 percent revenue and earnings growth equally from acquisitions and technology services, David Demshur told Reuters in an interview.

But he said a rally in world oil prices to five-year highs had not translated into a windfall for oil service companies like Core because of a conservative approach by the energy industry following previous cycles of boom and bust.

Major oil companies account for about half of Core's revenues and demand for its analysis of reservoir rock and fluids is its fastest growing area, with a 17 percent jump this year in the amount of core it has analyzed, Demshur said.
Core from an oil or gas well is analyzed for its fluid and rock property and then its conditions are simulated in Core's laboratories to determine the best ways to boost output.
"Not only are they in major oil fields like the North Sea but we have a lot of companies in the U.S. going back into the fields that the majors sold," Demshur said.
The hottest growth areas for regional exploration studies were west Africa, Venezuela and the southern Caspian Sea, he said.
Lax environmental regulation outside the United States had also forced oil companies to take precautions against being penalized for health and safety problems at oil sites, he said.

"Oil companies right now have asked us to provide environmental testing services...because what they want to do is compile a background base record of what the environmental effects have been over the life of the field.
"They're doing this to protect themselves."
Demshur said Core had not benefited from the rally in oil prices because most companies paid for its services out of their conservative development budgets, not their exploration budgets.
Crude oil, which is trading at $25 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange versus $17.50 a year ago, needed to stay at this level for a year to have a big impact on earnings, he said.

"Yes indeed we like oil with prices where they're at right now," Demshur, in London to visit European institutional investors, said. "It probably has some incremental effect but we don't think it's significant right now."
"Most oil company budgets as well as ours are figured around $17-$18 a barrel...Everyone is very conservative this time around."

He said Core was reviewing three companies to buy but declined to give the names. "Although Core Laboratories has enjoyed significant progress as an independent company, we may be able to further enhance revenue and profit by aligning with larger more integrated oilfield service companies," he said.
The company went public a year ago at $12 a share and is now trading on the Nasdaq at $15-3/4.

Demshur said he was comfortable with analysts' third and fourth quarter earnings per share estimates of $0.22 and $0.23-$0.24 respectively. That is up from $0.15 in the third quarter of last year and $0.19 in the fourth.
Richard Bergmark, chief financial officer, said Core's price/earnings ratio of 17.6 on analysts' 1996 estimates was at a discount to a comparative group of four companies' of 25.8.
Based on analysts' 1997 projections, Core was also trading at a discount to the peer group with 15.3 versus 19.9, he said.
Jefferies & Co analysts Byron Dunn and Sam Albright on Tuesday downgraded their rating for Core Laboratories to accumulate from buy.
-- John Hanley, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8185
